newsitem.title: UK: Oil steady as traders await progress on Iraq sales.
newsitem.headline: Oil steady as traders await progress on Iraq sales.

text.p: World oil markets moved sideways on Thursday with business dulled by a reluctance to trade without further firm news on when Iraq will resume crude exports.
London bellwether Brent futures were unchanged by 1700 GMT at $18.39 a barrel.

Traders want clear guidance on when Iraq will start selling oil under the second phase of an agreement allowing Baghdad limited oil exports in return for aid to alleviate civilian suffering as a result of international sanctions.
Members of the United Nations sanctions committee on Iraq said on Thursday that Baghdad would not receive permission to change deadlines for selling its $2 billion "oil-for-food" accord allotment.
The firm line by the committee means that Baghdad will be held to the accord's requirement to export around $1 billion by early September or forego part of the oil sales altogether.

"The resolution says up to $1 billion (in each 90 days of the accord) in exports. It is up to them to decide how much they want to export. They have put themselves in a disadvantageous position," said a senior Western diplomat.
Another senior Western diplomat said if a request by Iraq for flexibility came before the Security Council it would be denied.
"The Security Council would turn around and say: 'you put yourselves in this position,'" the diplomat said.
Diplomats threw cold water on speculation in the oil market that Iraq might be allowed some flexibility in order to ease oil sales which have been delayed since early June.

Iraq has been allowed to sell oil since June 8 under a second round of the accord, but has held up oil sales until its aid distribution plan was finalised, apparently as a protest at U.N. delays in approving aid imports during the first round.

Meanwhile a new plan for aid distribution under the deal is under review by the U.N. Secretariat and is expected to be approved by the end of July, according to senior U.N. Department of Humanitarian Aid (DHA) officials.
A new pricing formula and oil sales contracts must then be approved, a process that should be speedy if Iraq rolls over terms and contracts which applied in the first round.

Oil industry participants figure that Baghdad would need to export from 1.5 to two million barrels per day (bpd) in order to reach the $1 billion total before the September 5 deadline. Exports averaged a little over 660,000 bpd in the first round.
